nodes.notes:
Planning Projects pt1

Planning Projects

Purpose - Guides project execution 

Should be realistic and useful

Project Integration Management - Knowledge area that involves coordinating all the project knowledge areas throughout a project’s lifespan

Project Management Plan - Document used to integrate all other project documents and guide execution, monitoring and control

Facilitates communication among stakeholders

Serves as a baseline for measurement and control

A starting point to reference for future comparison

Should be dynamic and flexible

Project Scope Management - Determines how scope will be defined, validated, and controlled

Verification - Deliverable complies with given requirements and specifications

Quality Control

Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) - Table that lists requirements and various attributes on how close we are to meeting those requirements

Validation - Formal acceptance of the deliverables by the customers and other stakeholders

Defining Scope - Exactly what the project is expected to accomplish

May need to be updated as project progresses

Scope Creep - Scope becoming larger as project continues

Avoiding Scope Creep

Know project

Document Requirements

Change Control Processes

Avoid Gold Plating - Always wanting to make things just a liiiiiitttle bit better

Work Breakdown Structure - Deliverable-oriented grouping of the work involved in a project that defines the total scope of the project.

Breaks down all work into discrete tasks

Work Package - Deliverable at the lowest level of the WBS

100% of all deliverables should be included in WBS

Graphical Form

Entire project in Level 1

Main Groupings in Level 2

Smaller groupings further down

All blocks are nouns which is cool i guess



Tabular form

Same information, presented in a list

A good WBS is Mutually Exclusive Completely Exhaustive

nodes.notes:
Chapter 5 - Planning Projects pt2

Schedule and Cost

Project Planning (Review) - Guides project execution

Project Schedule Management

Schedule management plan - details how the schedule will be managed

Defining Activities

Activity - Distinct, scheduled portion of work performed during a project

Activity List - Tabular list of activities to be included on a project schedule

Defined by identifying activities required to create each work package on the WBS

WBS 100% Rule - Once you complete all the work for the work packages, the project should be done

Date the completion of each work package

Interim Deliverables - Deliverables needed to create the final product, but are discarded after project completion

Ex. Program for internal testing during development

Work packages - Deliverables

Milestone List

Milestone - significant point or event in a project

Generally encompass many completed activities

Should be developed early

Small and frequent

Binary

Completed or missed

Activity - Work

Deliverable - Output

Milestone - Marker for progress

Should be SMART

Specific

Measurable

Attainable

Relevant

Time-framed

Sequencing and Planning

Dependencies

Reason

Mandatory - Inherent within nature of project

Ex. Can’t hold training classes until training materials are ready

Discretionary - Defined by project team

Ex. Don’t start working until project is signed off on

External - Defined by someone outside project team

Ex. Can’t start development until supplies are delivered

Internal - Within team’s control

Ex. Must build a machine before testing it

Type

Finish-to-Start - Task B cannot start until Task A is finished

Most common (90%)

Start-to-Start - Task B cannot start until Task A is started

Finish-to-Finish - Task B cannot finish until Task A is finished

Start-to-Finish - Task B cannot finish until Task A is started

Rarely used

Estimating Resources

Duration Estimating

Duration - Total amount of elapsed time from activity start to finish

Used to determine schedule

Discrete - Exact value estimate

Range estimate

3-point Estimate - Optimistic, most likely, AND pessimistic values for duration



Lead Time - Time you can start an activity before its prerequisite is done

Negative

Lag Time - Time after an activity has been completed before you can start the next one

Positive

Effort - Amount of time spent working to complete a task

Used to determine labor costs

Gantt Charts 

Bar chart based on prerequisites and activity durations





Project Networks

Objective - Minimize project completion time

Uses a network diagram

Activity-on-Arrow Approach

Activities represented by arcs

Can only be used by finish-start dependencies

(kind of suck, won't be explaining)

Activity-on-Node Approach

Also called Precedence Diagramming Method

Activities represented by nodes

Used by PM software





Largest, so duration is 38

Critical Activities - B-D-E-F

Critical Path Method

2 Passes - One forward, one backward









Critical Activities - Those with 0 Slack

No wiggle room before required start and earliest start

1:18:00 (Video)

Critical Path - Shortest time in which project can be completed

Cannot delay any project along path without delaying project

Schedule Compression

Crashing - Making cost and schedule trade-offs to obtain the optimal amount of compression-cost tradeoff

Ex. Pay $1000 to shorten Activity 1 by a week

Fast Tracking - Doing activities in parallel that would normally be done in sequence

Risky, can backfire

Multitasking - One resource works on more than one project at the time time

Delays each individual part

Buffer - Built in extra time to complete a task

Project buffer - Buffer to complete an entire project

Feeding Buffer - Buffer before critical activities on non-critical activities (see lecture)

Parkinson’s Law - Work expands to fit allotted time

Cost Estimates

Analogous Estimates - Estimation by comparing to actual costs of a similar project	

Top-down

Bottom-Up - Estimate the cost of each activity, then adding them all up

Parametric Modeling - Based on estimated costs of materials to complete tasks

Cost Budgeting - Produces a cost baseline

Time-phased budget











































Olympics Video

1000 Nodes

15-20 Planners

5-6 Interface

207000 milestones

700 key milestones

nodes.notes:
Intro

file:///C:/Users/taylo/Downloads/Topic%201%20-%20Intro%20to%20PM.pdf



Project Management

Project Management - The application of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to project activities to meet project requirement

Project - A temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result

Temporary

End when output is produced

Fixed Budget

Attributes of Projects

Projects have a unique purpose

Ex. build THIS specific house with THESE requirements

Temporary, definite beginning and end

Drive change, or enable value creation

Developed iteratively

Require resources

Have a primary customer or sponsor

Someone responsible for direction and funding of the project

Involve uncertainty

Project Constraints

Triple Constraint

Scope - What needs to be done and how should it be done?

Schedule - How long should it take to be completed?

Cost - What is the budget? What resources should be needed?

Quality 

Sometimes included in the Quadruple Constraint

Risk

Resources

Project Stakeholders - Any person involved in or affected by the project

Ex. Couple wanting to build a home

Project Sponsor - Responsible for direction and funding of the project

Couple

Project Manager - Lead the operations of the project

Contractor

Project Team - Those involved in Project completion

Employees

Support Staff - Support project team

Business office workers

Suppliers

Additional Stakeholders

Opponents

Defining Project Success

Did the project meet the triple constraint?

Was the sponsor satisfied?

Can also be measured by customer rating system

Did the project produce the desired results?

May not be immediately known if desired results are long term

Not everything is a project, some things are Operations

Ongoing/permanent activities

Help sustain business, make profit

Day-to-day things

Programs and Portfolios

Program - a group of related projects managed in a coordinated manner to obtain benefits that would not be apparent if managed individually

Ex. A construction company building small homes and large office buildings at the same time

Not necessarily a megaproject, (one large >$1bn project)

Portfolio Management - The way in which organization group and manage projects and programs

Concerned not just with grouping projects, but with choosing the right projects to undertake

Generally done by higher level employees

Doing Project Management

Process Groups

Initiating

Planning

Executing

Monitoring/Controlling

Closing

Knowledge Areas

Integration Management

How the project fits together

Project management software, change requests, lesson-learned reports

Scope Management

Score statements, work breakdown structures, requirements analyses

Schedule

PERT, GANTT charts

Cost

Quality

Resources

Communication

Kickoff meetings, status and progress reports

Risk

Procurement

Stakeholders

Project Managers

Should be proficient in all 10 knowledge areas

Proficiency in application area

Knowledge of Project Environment

Politics, culture

General business knowledge

Human relations

Soft skills increasingly important today

Talent Triangle

Technical Skills

Soft Skills

Leader - Focuses on long term goals and inspires people

Leadership Styles

Laissez-Faire - Hands off

Transactional - Step in to offer reward or reinforcement

Servant - Focus on building community

Transformational - Inspire others and empower them to get things done

Charismatic - Lead by enthusiasm

Interactional - Transactional, transformational, AND charismatic

Manager - Day to day details of meeting goals

Strategic and business skills

Certifications

Prince2 - UK/AU

PMP - USA

4500 hours of experience

CAPM 

1500 hours of experience or 23 hours of training

nodes.notes:
Chapter 6 - Project Planning pt3

Remaining Knowledge Areas

Project Quality Management

Quality - Degree to which set of inherent characteristics fulfills requirements

Conformance to requirements - Processes and products meet written specifications

Fitness for use - Product or process can be used as intended

Customer decides if quality is satisfactory

Many fail cause they consider only the written requirements, ignore other stakeholder needs and expectations.

Quality Management Plan - Identifying quality standards and how to meet them

Metric - Standard of metric

Failure rate, availability, customer satisfaction ratings

Schedule - Completing the project on time

Customer Satisfaction

Cost Reduction - Recouping project costs

Project Dashboard - Keeps track of all metrics on one graphic

Project Resource Management

Project Organizational Chart - Keeps track of who does what

Responsibility Assignment Matrix - Maps the tasks of the WBS to people responsible for performing that work

RACI Chart

Responsible - Does the Task

Only one per task

Accountable - Signs off on the task

Consulted - Has information needed to complete task

Informed - need to be notified of task results

Staffing Management Plan - Described how people are added and removed from a project

Team Charter - Promotes teamwork and clarifies how team will communicate

Can be completed within a 1-2hr meeting

What do we do if there is a problem?

Project Communications Management

Communications Management Plan - Document that guides communication

Project Stakeholder Management

Project Risk Management

Uncertainty that can have a positive or negative effect on meeting objectives

Cannot manage risks until you identify them

Probability Impact Matrix - Classifies risks by likelihood and how bad they will be

Top right is the worst

Low left, no matter

Risk Avoidance - Eliminate causes of risk

Risk Acceptance - Accepting the consequences, if the risk occurs

Risk Transference - Transfer consequences to a third party

Insurance

Risk Mitigation - Reduce Likelihood

Positive Risks

Risk Exploitation - Trying to make sure a risk happens

Risk Sharing - Allocation ownership of risk to another party

Risk enhancement - Increase size of opportunity

Risk Acceptance - Dont care to seize opportunity, if it happens it happens

Contingency Plan - Outlined actions if a specific risk event occurs

Fallback Plan - For risks that have a high impact on meeting objectives. Last resort

Contingency Reserves - Money to alleviate effects of risks

Allowances

Project Procurement Management

Make-or-Buy Analysis - Produce internally or outsource?

Contract

Termination Clause - How to get out of contract, what will happen if you do

Incentive Clause - Gives bonuses for behaving in good ways

Liquidated Damages Clause - What happens if seller does not do what supposed to do

Fixed Price Contract - Seller provides product at a fixed price, does not rise/fall with market price

Competitive Contract - Many given small task, best performers get big contract

Cost Reimbursable - Pay some directly, and some indirect costs

Electricity, rent, etc

Time and Material - Pay a fixed price for materials, and an hourly wage for labor

Unit Price - Predetermined price per unit of service

Procurement Documents

Request for Proposal (RFP) - Seller offers a proposal on how they will  meet your goals

Open ended

Request for Quote (RFQ) - Sellers offers a price for what they will provide

Predefined

Statement of Work (SOW) - What you need provided

Supplier Evaluation Matrix - Weights the suppliers based on different weighted categories



Titanic Video

Competitor action to deliver Olmpic and Titanic

Lowering market share, competition, luxury service

Payback Period for White Flint

2yr

Number of Lifeboats change, why?

48 to 16, didnt want to worry customers

How did incidents with Olympic impact Titanic

Replacement teams were taken from titanic workers

How did Titanic Crash Crew schedule to stay on time for completion

Rush, third shifts

Feedback to detect icebergs, what went wrong?

No binoculars, fudged rests

nodes.notes:
Chapter 7 - Executing Projects

Project Execution

Most noticed processed group

Most time, money, and results

Project Integration Management

Most important output of a project is its deliverables

Management by Walking Around (MBWA) - Talk to employees, see how project is going

Issue Log - logs issues

Matter under question that could impede project success

Common issues

Upper management not supporting

Team not significantly involved

Conflict Handling

Collaboration Mode - Directly face conflict and allow parties to work through disagreement

Compromise - give and take approach, give satisfaction to all

Smoothing or Accommodating - Suppress areas of disagreement, emphasize areas of agreement

Force or Direct - You’re wrong, i'm right

Withdraw - Ignore problem, avoidance



Conflict can avoid groupthink

Conformance to what you think the group wants

Task-related conflict, difference over team objectives, is positive

Emotional conflict, personal disagreements, is negative

Project Quality Management

Quality Assurance - all activities relevant to satisfying quality standards

Benchmarking - Compares to other similar projects

Quality audit - Helps identify lessons learned and improve performance

Cause and effect diagrams - find root causes of problems

Fishbone or ishikawa diagrams

Kanban - Just in time approach

Sign - Signal when things need to be done

Motivation

Intrinsic - Motivation for own enjoyment

Extrinsic - Motivation by reward or punishment

Motivational Factors - Factors that cause job satisfaction

Hygiene Factors - Factors that will not cause satisfaction, but will cause dissatisfaction if they are not there

McClelland Acquired Needs-Theory

Achievement

Affiliation

Power

Douglas McGregor

Theory X - People avoid work

Theory Y - People naturally want to work

Cognitive Work

Higher reward = lower performance

Autonomy - Desire to be self directed

Mastery

Purpose

Habits of Highly Effective People

Be proactive

Begin with the end in mind

Put the first things first

Think win-win - for you to win, someone else has to lose

Seek first to understand, then to be understood

Synergize

Sharpen the Saw

Managing Projects

Managers can best help by inputting expertise and work challenge

Fail when relying on authority, money, or penalty

Good managers are empathic listeners - listen with intent to understand

Have rapport - Support of team

Mirroring - Matching behaviors to person you are talking to

Staff Assignment

Resource Loading - Amount of resources a schedule requires during specific time periods

Overallocation - Assigning more work to an employee that can be done

Resource Levelling - Resolving resource conflict by delaying tasks

Assessing Team Performance

Stages

Forming - Getting to know each other

Storming - Exchange differences of opinions

Norming - Developing a common method of flow for the team

Performing - Getting job done

Adjourning - Ending team

Social Styles Profile

Drivers - proactive and task oriented

Expressive - proactive and people oriented

Analyticals - Reactive and task oriented

Amiables - Reactive and people oriented

Put good news in writing, bad news in person

Project Procurement Management

Source Selection

Approach one supplier

Approach a few supplier

Advertise to many sellers

Short list - List of 3-5 top best sellers

Prepare a best-and-final offer

nodes.excerpt: BIT 4484 Notes 8 9 2020 covers monitoring, controlling, and closing projects.
nodes.notes:
Monitoring and Controlling - Chapter 8

Monitoring and Controlling

Expert Judgement - Your own intuition

Main tool and technique for monitoring and controlling

Earned Value Management

Measures project performance based on scope, schedule, and cost

Planned Value (PV)- Portion of approved total cost estimate that was planned to have been spent during a given period

Actual Costs (AC) - Total costs that were actually incurred

Rate of Performance (RP) - Amount of work completed as a proportion of work expected to be completed at given time

Earned Value (EV) - Estimate of the value of work performed in given period



Calculations

Cost Variance (CV) - Compared budgeted cost vs actual costs



Schedule Variance (SV) - Compared work performed vs actual work performed 

SV = EV - PV

Cost Performance Index - Financial effectiveness of a project

CPI = EV / AC

> 1 is good

Schedule Performance Index - How close the project is to schedule

SPI = EV / PV

> 1 is good

Estimate at Completion - Best guess for how much money will be spent at the end of the project

Project Scope Management

Scope Creep - tendency of scope to increase over time

Wasa Video

Wasa - a warship

Changes

Speed up ship

Increase to 120 feet

Changed to 111

Needed double cannons

Needed much more space

Died of a heart attack after all changes

Ship sunk after 15 minutes

Project Schedule Management

Know the status of the schedule

Influence the factors that can cause schedule issues

Determine whether the schedule has changed

Manage changes when they occur

Slipped Milestone - A milestone reached later than expected

What do sponsors hate most?

Surprises

Be clear and honest with sponsors 

Control Charts - Illustrate results of a process over time

Seven Run Rule - Examine if there is a problem if there are 7 data points in a row above/below mean

Pareto Chart - Bar chart with cumulative percentage as line

80%/20% rule - 80% of problems come from 20% of causes

Stratification - separate data to see patterns

Project Risk Management

Workarounds - Unplanned responses to risk events 

Project Procurement Management

Constructive Change Orders - Oral or written requests made by someone with authority

Project Cost Management

To-Complete Performance Index



Examples



Closing Projects - Chapter 9 

Closing

Closing Methods

Integration - Project completed successfully, integrated into operations

Most common

Addition - New unit added to company as result of project

Extinction - Project done, no addition or integration

Extinction by murder - Higher up kills project

Starvation - Project ends by stopping funding

Withdrawal of life support

Outputs

Transition plan - Final product, processes, and instructions to use them

Lessons Learned Report - Major takeaways for a future project

Close-out Meeting

Opposite of a kickoff meeting

Includes major stakeholders

Knowledge Transfer - Sharing of knowledge gained during project

Employee knowledge, human capital, is the key asset of company

Challenger

Failure with O-Ring

People at lower levels could not communicate with top levels

nodes.name: Certifications
nodes.excerpt: Certifications in project management include Prince2, PMP, and CAPM.
nodes.notes: Certifications in project management include Prince2 (UK/AU), PMP (USA, requiring 4500 hours of experience), and CAPM (requiring 1500 hours of experience or 23 hours of training). These certifications validate a project manager's expertise.
nodes.context_summary:
- Certifications include Prince2, PMP, and CAPM.
- PMP requires 4500 hours of experience.
- CAPM requires 1500 hours of experience or 23 hours of training.
- Certifications validate a project manager's expertise.

nodes.name: Closing Methods
nodes.excerpt: Closing Methods describe how projects are concluded, including integration, addition, extinction, and starvation.
nodes.notes: Closing Methods in project management include Integration, where the project is successfully completed and integrated into operations; Addition, where a new unit is added to the company; Extinction, where the project is completed with no further additions; and Starvation, where the project ends due to lack of funding. These methods are crucial for formal project closure.
context_summary: - Describe how projects are concluded.
- Include Integration, Addition, Extinction, and Starvation.
- Integration involves successful project completion.
- Addition adds a new unit to the company.
- Extinction ends the project with no further additions.
- Starvation ends the project due to lack of funding.

nodes.name: Cognitive Work
nodes.excerpt: Cognitive Work suggests that higher rewards can lead to lower performance.
nodes.notes: Cognitive Work theory posits that for tasks requiring cognitive effort, higher monetary rewards can paradoxically lead to lower performance. It emphasizes the importance of autonomy, mastery, and purpose in motivating individuals.
nodes.context_summary:
- Higher monetary rewards can lower performance.
- Emphasizes autonomy, mastery, and purpose in motivation.

nodes.name: Conflict Handling
nodes.excerpt: Conflict Handling involves various strategies to manage disagreements within a project team.
nodes.notes: Conflict Handling in project management includes strategies such as Collaboration Mode, Compromise, Smoothing or Accommodating, Force or Direct, and Withdraw. These strategies help manage disagreements and can prevent groupthink. Task-related conflict is seen as positive, while emotional conflict is negative.
nodes.context_summary:
- Involves strategies for managing disagreements.
- Strategies include Collaboration, Compromise, Smoothing, Force, and Withdraw.
- Task-related conflict is positive; emotional conflict is negative.

nodes.name: Control Charts
nodes.excerpt: Control Charts illustrate the results of a process over time.
nodes.notes: Control Charts are used in project management to monitor process performance over time. They help identify trends and variations, and the Seven Run Rule is applied to detect potential issues when there are seven consecutive data points above or below the mean.
context_summary: - Illustrate process results over time.
- Used to monitor process performance.
- Help identify trends and variations.
- Apply the Seven Run Rule for detecting issues.

nodes.name: Cost Estimates
nodes.excerpt: Cost Estimates are predictions of the costs involved in completing project activities.
nodes.notes: Cost Estimates can be derived using various methods such as analogous estimates, bottom-up estimates, and parametric modeling. These estimates help in creating a cost baseline and are essential for budgeting and financial planning.
nodes.context_summary:
- Predictions of costs for completing project activities.
- Derived using methods like analogous estimates and bottom-up estimates.
- Essential for budgeting and financial planning.

nodes.name: Critical Path Method
nodes.excerpt: The Critical Path Method is used to determine the shortest project duration.
nodes.notes: The Critical Path Method identifies critical activities with zero slack that cannot be delayed without affecting the project completion date. It involves two passes through the project network: one forward and one backward.
nodes.context_summary:
- Used to determine the shortest project duration.
- Identifies critical activities with zero slack.
- Involves two passes through the project network: forward and backward.

nodes.name: Dependencies
nodes.excerpt: Dependencies are logical relationships between project activities.
nodes.notes: Dependencies define the order of activities in a project. They can be mandatory, discretionary, external, or internal, and are categorized by type: Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, and Start-to-Finish.
nodes.context_summary:
- Define logical relationships between project activities.
- Determine the order of activities.
- Can be mandatory, discretionary, external, or internal.
- Categorized by type: Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, Start-to-Finish.

nodes.name: Directive Project
nodes.excerpt: Directive Projects are mandatory projects that must be executed.
nodes.notes: Directive Projects are those that an organization is required to undertake, often due to regulatory requirements or strategic directives. These projects are non-negotiable and must be completed as directed.
context_summary: - Directive Projects are mandatory and must be executed.
- They are often due to regulatory requirements or strategic directives.

nodes.name: Discretionary Costs
nodes.excerpt: Discretionary Costs are optional expenses that can be adjusted.
nodes.notes: Discretionary Costs refer to expenses that are not essential and can be adjusted or eliminated based on the organization's financial strategy. These costs are often associated with projects that are not critical to the core operations.
context_summary: - Discretionary Costs are optional expenses.
- They can be adjusted or eliminated based on financial strategy.

nodes.name: Douglas McGregor Theory X and Theory Y
nodes.excerpt: Douglas McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y describe two contrasting views of workforce motivation.
nodes.notes: Douglas McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y present two different views of individuals at work: Theory X assumes people inherently dislike work and must be coerced, while Theory Y assumes people are self-motivated and enjoy work.
nodes.context_summary:
- Theory X assumes people dislike work.
- Theory Y assumes people are self-motivated.
- Presents contrasting views of workforce motivation.

nodes.name: Earned Value Management
nodes.excerpt: Earned Value Management measures project performance based on scope, schedule, and cost.
nodes.notes: Earned Value Management is a key tool and technique for monitoring and controlling projects. It involves calculations such as Planned Value (PV), Actual Costs (AC), Rate of Performance (RP), and Earned Value (EV). It helps in determining Cost Variance (CV) and Schedule Variance (SV), and uses indices like Cost Performance Index (CPI) and Schedule Performance Index (SPI) to assess project financial effectiveness and schedule adherence.
context_summary: - Measures project performance based on scope, schedule, and cost.
- Involves calculations like Planned Value (PV) and Actual Costs (AC).
- Determines Cost Variance (CV) and Schedule Variance (SV).
- Uses Cost Performance Index (CPI) and Schedule Performance Index (SPI).

nodes.name: Financial Considerations
nodes.excerpt: Financial considerations include NPV, ROI, and payback period.
nodes.notes:
Financial considerations in project selection involve evaluating the net present value (NPV), return on investment (ROI), and payback period of projects. These metrics help in assessing the financial viability and potential returns of projects.

Financial considerations include assigning weights to each financial metric to calculate a weighted score for project evaluation.

Financial Considerations include Net Present Value, Return on Investment, and Payback Period. These are used to assess the financial viability and potential returns of projects.

Financial considerations include Net Present Value (NPV), Return on Investment (ROI), and Payback Period, which are used to assess the financial viability and potential returns of projects.

Financial considerations also include the calculation of a weighted score for each project by assigning weights to each financial metric.
context_summary: - Financial considerations include NPV, ROI, and payback period.
- They assess the financial viability and potential returns of projects.

nodes.name: Habits of Highly Effective People
nodes.excerpt: The Habits of Highly Effective People include proactive behavior and seeking mutual benefit.
nodes.notes: The Habits of Highly Effective People include being proactive, beginning with the end in mind, prioritizing important tasks, thinking win-win, seeking first to understand then to be understood, synergizing, and continuous self-improvement.
nodes.context_summary:
- Includes proactive behavior.
- Encourages beginning with the end in mind.
- Promotes prioritizing important tasks and seeking mutual benefit.

nodes.name: Issue Log
nodes.excerpt: An Issue Log is used to document issues that could impede project success.
nodes.notes: The Issue Log is a tool used in project management to document and track issues that arise during a project. It helps in identifying matters that could impede project success and ensures they are addressed in a timely manner.
nodes.context_summary:
- Documents issues in project management.
- Tracks matters that could impede success.
- Ensures timely addressing of issues.

nodes.name: Knowledge Transfer
nodes.excerpt: Knowledge Transfer involves sharing knowledge gained during a project.
nodes.notes: Knowledge Transfer is essential during project closure, ensuring that lessons learned and key insights are communicated to stakeholders and future project teams. It emphasizes the importance of human capital as a key asset.
context_summary: - Involves sharing knowledge gained during a project.
- Essential during project closure.
- Ensures communication of lessons learned.
- Emphasizes human capital as a key asset.

nodes.name: Leadership Styles
nodes.excerpt: Leadership styles in project management include laissez-faire, transactional, servant, transformational, charismatic, and interactional.
nodes.notes: Leadership styles in project management include laissez-faire (hands-off), transactional (reward-based), servant (community-focused), transformational (inspirational), charismatic (enthusiasm-driven), and interactional (a combination of transactional, transformational, and charismatic).
nodes.context_summary:
- Leadership styles include laissez-faire, transactional, servant, transformational, charismatic, and interactional.
- Laissez-faire is hands-off.
- Transactional is reward-based.
- Servant leadership is community-focused.
- Transformational leadership is inspirational.
- Charismatic leadership is enthusiasm-driven.
- Interactional combines various styles.

nodes.name: Management by Walking Around (MBWA)
nodes.excerpt: Management by Walking Around involves managers talking to employees to see how a project is progressing.
nodes.notes: Management by Walking Around (MBWA) is a management style where managers walk around in an unstructured manner through the workplace, engaging with employees to understand how projects are progressing and to identify any issues firsthand.
nodes.context_summary:
- Managers engage with employees.
- They assess project progress.
- Issues are identified firsthand.

nodes.name: McClelland Acquired Needs Theory
nodes.excerpt: McClelland's Acquired Needs Theory identifies three motivators: Achievement, Affiliation, and Power.
nodes.notes: McClelland's Acquired Needs Theory suggests that individuals are motivated by three needs: Achievement, Affiliation, and Power. These needs drive behavior and influence how people are motivated in a work environment.
nodes.context_summary:
- Identifies three motivators: Achievement, Affiliation, Power.
- These needs drive behavior in the workplace.

nodes.name: Milestone List
nodes.excerpt: The Milestone List includes significant points or events in a project.
nodes.notes: Milestones are significant points or events in a project that generally encompass many completed activities. They should be developed early, be small and frequent, and are binary in nature (completed or missed). Milestones should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-framed.
nodes.context_summary:
- Includes significant points or events in a project.
- Encompasses many completed activities.
- Should be developed early and be small and frequent.
- Milestones are binary (completed or missed).
- Must be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-framed.

nodes.name: Pareto Chart
nodes.excerpt: A Pareto Chart is a bar chart with a cumulative percentage line.
nodes.notes: The Pareto Chart is used to identify the most significant factors in a dataset, following the 80/20 rule where 80% of problems are caused by 20% of causes. It helps prioritize issues for resolution.
context_summary: - A bar chart with a cumulative percentage line.
- Identifies significant factors in a dataset.
- Follows the 80/20 rule for problem causes.
- Helps prioritize issues for resolution.

nodes.name: Portfolio Management
nodes.excerpt: Portfolio Management involves grouping and managing projects and programs.
nodes.notes: Portfolio Management is concerned with grouping and managing projects and programs, focusing on choosing the right projects to undertake. It is generally done by higher-level employees.
nodes.context_summary:
- Portfolio Management involves grouping projects and programs.
- It focuses on choosing the right projects to undertake.
- Generally managed by higher-level employees.

nodes.name: Process Groups
nodes.excerpt: Process Groups in project management include initiating, planning, executing, monitoring/controlling, and closing.
nodes.notes: Process Groups in project management consist of initiating, planning, executing, monitoring/controlling, and closing. These groups help structure the project management process.
nodes.context_summary:
- Process Groups include initiating, planning, executing, monitoring/controlling, and closing.
- They help structure the project management process.

nodes.name: Program
nodes.excerpt: A Program is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated manner.
nodes.notes: A Program consists of related projects managed together to obtain benefits not apparent if managed individually. It is not necessarily a megaproject, which is a single large project over $1 billion.
nodes.context_summary:
- A Program is a group of related projects.
- Programs are managed in a coordinated manner.
- Benefits are obtained that are not apparent when projects are managed individually.

nodes.name: Project Communications Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Communications Management guides how project information is communicated.
nodes.notes: Project Communications Management involves guiding how project information is communicated. The Communications Management Plan is a document that guides communication within the project.
nodes.context_summary:
- Guides communication of project information.
- Includes Communications Management Plan.

nodes.name: Project Integration Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Integration Management coordinates all project knowledge areas throughout a project's lifespan.
nodes.notes:
Project Integration Management is a knowledge area that involves coordinating all the project knowledge areas throughout a project’s lifespan. It ensures that various elements of the project are properly aligned and integrated.

The most important output of a project is its deliverables, highlighting the role of Project Integration Management in ensuring these are achieved.
nodes.context_summary:
- Coordinates all project knowledge areas.
- Ensures alignment and integration throughout the project lifespan.
- Focuses on achieving project deliverables.

nodes.name: Project Management Plan
nodes.excerpt: The Project Management Plan integrates all project documents and guides execution, monitoring, and control.
nodes.notes: The Project Management Plan is a document used to integrate all other project documents and guide execution, monitoring, and control. It facilitates communication among stakeholders, serves as a baseline for measurement and control, and acts as a starting point for future comparison. It should be dynamic and flexible.
nodes.context_summary:
- Integrates all project documents
- Guides execution, monitoring, and control
- Facilitates communication among stakeholders
- Serves as a baseline for measurement and control
- Dynamic and flexible document

nodes.name: Project Portfolio Selection
nodes.excerpt: Project portfolio selection focuses on projects providing the most business value.
nodes.notes:
Project portfolio selection involves choosing projects that provide the most business value, including venture projects for innovation, growth projects for revenue increase, and core projects for maintaining business operations.

Project Portfolio Selection involves selecting projects that provide the most business value, including venture, growth, and core projects.

Project Portfolio Selection includes selecting projects that provide the most business value, such as venture projects for innovation, growth projects for revenue increase, and core projects for maintaining business operations.

Project portfolio selection involves selecting projects that provide the most business value, including venture projects for innovation, growth projects for revenue increase, and core projects for maintaining operations.

Project portfolio selection includes venture projects, which are new and innovative, growth projects that help increase revenue, and core projects that maintain business operations.
context_summary: - Project portfolio selection focuses on projects providing business value.
- It includes venture projects for innovation, growth projects for revenue increase, and core projects for maintaining operations.

nodes.name: Project Procurement Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Procurement Management involves acquiring goods and services from external sources.
nodes.notes:
Project Procurement Management involves acquiring goods and services from external sources. It includes Make-or-Buy Analysis, various contract types (Fixed Price, Competitive, Cost Reimbursable, Time and Material, Unit Price), and procurement documents like RFP, RFQ, and SOW. The Supplier Evaluation Matrix is used to evaluate suppliers based on weighted categories.

Source Selection involves different approaches to selecting suppliers, such as approaching one supplier, a few suppliers, or advertising to many sellers. A shortlist of 3-5 top sellers is prepared for final offers.

Constructive Change Orders are oral or written requests made by someone with authority.
context_summary: - Involves acquiring goods and services from external sources.
- Includes Make-or-Buy Analysis and various contract types.
- Uses procurement documents like RFP and RFQ.
- Employs the Supplier Evaluation Matrix for supplier evaluation.
- Source Selection can involve different approaches.
- Prepares a shortlist of 3-5 top sellers for final offers.

nodes.name: Project Quality Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Quality Management ensures that a project meets the required quality standards.
nodes.notes:
Project Quality Management involves ensuring that a project meets the required quality standards. It includes conformance to requirements, fitness for use, and customer satisfaction. Many projects fail because they only consider written requirements and ignore other stakeholder needs and expectations. The Quality Management Plan identifies quality standards and how to meet them.

Quality Assurance encompasses all activities relevant to satisfying quality standards, including benchmarking and quality audits. Cause and effect diagrams, such as fishbone or Ishikawa diagrams, are used to find root causes of problems.
nodes.context_summary:
- Ensures projects meet quality standards.
- Includes conformance to requirements and customer satisfaction.
- Quality Management Plan identifies standards and methods to meet them.

nodes.name: Project Resource Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Resource Management involves organizing and managing the project team.
nodes.notes: Project Resource Management involves organizing and managing the project team. It includes the Project Organizational Chart, which tracks who does what, and the Responsibility Assignment Matrix, which maps tasks to people responsible for performing them. The RACI Chart defines roles such as Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed. The Staffing Management Plan describes how people are added and removed from a project, and the Team Charter promotes teamwork and clarifies communication.
nodes.context_summary:
- Organizes and manages the project team.
- Includes Project Organizational Chart.
- Uses Responsibility Assignment Matrix.
- Defines roles with RACI Chart.
- Staffing Management Plan describes team changes.
- Team Charter promotes teamwork and communication.

nodes.name: Project Risk Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Risk Management involves identifying and managing project risks.
nodes.notes:
Project Risk Management involves identifying and managing project risks. It includes the Probability Impact Matrix, which classifies risks by likelihood and impact. Strategies include Risk Avoidance, Acceptance, Transference, and Mitigation. Positive risks can be managed through Exploitation, Sharing, Enhancement, and Acceptance. Contingency and Fallback Plans are prepared for specific risk events, and Contingency Reserves are set aside to alleviate risk effects.

Workarounds are unplanned responses to risk events.
context_summary: - Involves identifying and managing project risks.
- Uses the Probability Impact Matrix for classification.
- Strategies include Avoidance, Acceptance, Transference, and Mitigation.
- Positive risks can be managed through Exploitation and Sharing.
- Prepares Contingency and Fallback Plans.
- Sets aside Contingency Reserves for risk effects.

nodes.name: Project Schedule Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Schedule Management involves planning, developing, managing, and controlling the project schedule.
nodes.notes:
Project Schedule Management includes creating a schedule management plan, defining activities, sequencing them, estimating resources and durations, and controlling the schedule. It involves using tools like Gantt charts and network diagrams to optimize project timelines.

Includes managing changes when they occur and addressing slipped milestones, which are milestones reached later than expected.
context_summary: - Involves planning and controlling the project schedule.
- Includes creating a schedule management plan.
- Defines and sequences project activities.
- Uses tools like Gantt charts and network diagrams.
- Manages changes and addresses slipped milestones.

nodes.name: Project Scope Management
nodes.excerpt: Project Scope Management determines how scope will be defined, validated, and controlled.
nodes.notes:
Project Scope Management determines how scope will be defined, validated, and controlled. It includes processes such as verification, validation, and defining scope. It also addresses issues like scope creep and involves creating a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).

Scope creep is highlighted as a tendency for scope to increase over time, as illustrated by the Wasa warship example.
context_summary: - Determines how scope will be defined, validated, and controlled.
- Includes processes like verification and validation.
- Addresses scope creep issues.
- Involves creating a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).

nodes.name: Project Stakeholders
nodes.excerpt: Project Stakeholders are any persons involved in or affected by the project.
nodes.notes:
Project Stakeholders include anyone involved in or affected by the project, such as the project sponsor, project manager, project team, support staff, suppliers, and additional stakeholders like opponents.

Customer satisfaction is a key aspect of quality management, as customers decide if the quality is satisfactory. Many projects fail because they only consider written requirements and ignore other stakeholder needs and expectations.
nodes.context_summary:
- Includes anyone involved or affected by the project.
- Key stakeholders are project sponsor and manager.
- Involves project team and support staff.
- Suppliers and opponents are also stakeholders.
- Customer satisfaction is crucial for quality management.

nodes.name: Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)
nodes.excerpt: The Requirements Traceability Matrix lists requirements and tracks how closely they are met.
nodes.notes: The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) is a table that lists requirements and various attributes on how close the project is to meeting those requirements. It is a tool used in project scope management to ensure that all requirements are addressed.
nodes.context_summary:
- Lists project requirements
- Tracks how closely requirements are met
- Used in project scope management

nodes.name: Resource Allocation
nodes.excerpt: Resource Allocation involves distributing resources to selected projects.
nodes.notes: Resource Allocation is the process of distributing available resources to various projects that have been selected. It ensures that projects have the necessary resources to proceed and succeed.
context_summary: - Resource Allocation distributes resources to selected projects.
- It ensures projects have necessary resources to succeed.

nodes.name: Schedule Compression
nodes.excerpt: Schedule Compression involves techniques to shorten the project schedule.
nodes.notes: Schedule Compression includes techniques like crashing, which involves making cost and schedule trade-offs, and fast tracking, which involves doing activities in parallel that would normally be done in sequence. These techniques are used to meet project deadlines but can increase risk.
nodes.context_summary:
- Involves techniques to shorten the project schedule.
- Includes crashing and fast tracking.
- Can increase risk while meeting project deadlines.

nodes.name: Schedule Management Plan
nodes.excerpt: The Schedule Management Plan details how the project schedule will be managed.
nodes.notes: The Schedule Management Plan outlines the processes and tools used to manage the project schedule, including defining activities, sequencing, and estimating durations.
nodes.context_summary:
- Details how the project schedule will be managed.
- Outlines processes and tools for managing the project schedule.
- Includes defining activities and estimating durations.

nodes.name: Social Styles Profile
nodes.excerpt: The Social Styles Profile categorizes individuals as Drivers, Expressive, Analyticals, or Amiables.
nodes.notes: The Social Styles Profile is a framework for understanding interpersonal behavior. It categorizes individuals into four types: Drivers (proactive and task-oriented), Expressive (proactive and people-oriented), Analyticals (reactive and task-oriented), and Amiables (reactive and people-oriented).
nodes.context_summary:
- Categorizes individuals into four types: Drivers, Expressive, Analyticals, Amiables.
- Drivers are task-oriented; Expressive are people-oriented.
- Analyticals are reactive and task-oriented; Amiables are reactive and people-oriented.

nodes.name: Strategic Planning
nodes.excerpt: Strategic planning involves senior executives defining the vision or business plan and aligning projects with the overall strategy.
nodes.notes:
Strategic planning is often done by senior executives to define the vision or business plan of an organization. It is a critical step in aligning projects with the overall strategy.

Strategic planning is often done by senior executives who define the vision or business plan for the organization.

Strategic Planning is often conducted by senior executives to define the vision or business plan of an organization.

Strategic planning is often done by senior executives and involves defining the vision or business plan of an organization. It is crucial for aligning projects with the overall strategy.

Strategic planning is often conducted by senior executives to define the vision or business plan of an organization. It is crucial to ensure that projects align with the greater vision.
context_summary: - Strategic planning is conducted by senior executives.
- It defines the vision or business plan of an organization.
- It aligns projects with the overall strategy.

nodes.name: SWOT Analysis
nodes.excerpt: SWOT analysis evaluates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
nodes.notes:
SWOT analysis is a strategic planning tool used to identify and evaluate the internal strengths and weaknesses, as well as external opportunities and threats of a project or organization.

SWOT Analysis involves evaluating internal strengths and weaknesses, and external opportunities and threats.

SWOT Analysis involves evaluating internal strengths and weaknesses and identifying external opportunities and threats.

SWOT analysis involves evaluating internal strengths and weaknesses, and identifying external opportunities and threats.

SWOT analysis categorizes factors as internal (strengths and weaknesses) and external (opportunities and threats).
context_summary: - SWOT analysis evaluates internal strengths and weaknesses.
- It identifies external opportunities and threats.

nodes.name: Talent Triangle
nodes.excerpt: The Talent Triangle includes technical skills, soft skills, and strategic and business skills.
nodes.notes: The Talent Triangle in project management emphasizes the importance of technical skills, soft skills, and strategic and business skills. These skills are crucial for effective project management.
nodes.context_summary:
- The Talent Triangle includes technical skills, soft skills, and strategic/business skills.
- These skills are crucial for effective project management.

nodes.name: Titanic Video
nodes.excerpt: The Titanic Video discusses the competitive actions and challenges faced by the Titanic.
nodes.notes: The Titanic Video discusses the competitive actions to deliver the Olympic and Titanic, the impact of lowering market share, and the luxury service competition. It covers the payback period for White Flint, changes in the number of lifeboats, incidents with the Olympic affecting the Titanic, and the crash crew schedule to stay on time. Feedback issues in detecting icebergs are also highlighted.
nodes.context_summary:
- Discusses competitive actions for Titanic and Olympic.
- Covers impact of lowering market share.
- Highlights luxury service competition.
- Mentions payback period for White Flint.
- Discusses changes in lifeboat numbers.
- Addresses incidents with Olympic affecting Titanic.
- Covers crash crew schedule for timeliness.
- Highlights feedback issues in iceberg detection.

nodes.name: Triple Constraint
nodes.excerpt: The Triple Constraint in project management includes scope, schedule, and cost.
nodes.notes: The Triple Constraint in project management refers to the three primary constraints of scope, schedule, and cost. Quality is sometimes included as a fourth constraint, forming a Quadruple Constraint. These constraints are critical in defining project success.
nodes.context_summary:
- The Triple Constraint includes scope, schedule, and cost.
- Quality may be a fourth constraint.
- These constraints define project success.

nodes.name: Wasa Video
nodes.excerpt: The Wasa Video discusses the changes and challenges faced by the Wasa warship.
nodes.notes: The Wasa Video highlights the changes made to the Wasa warship, including increasing its length and adding double cannons, which ultimately led to its sinking. It serves as an example of scope creep and the consequences of unmanaged changes.
context_summary: - Discusses changes faced by the Wasa warship.
- Length of the warship was increased.
- Double cannons were added to the warship.
- The changes led to the warship's sinking.
- Serves as an example of scope creep.

nodes.name: Weighted Score
nodes.excerpt: Weighted Score involves assigning weights to financial considerations for project evaluation.
nodes.notes: The Weighted Score method involves assigning different weights to various financial considerations, such as NPV, ROI, and payback period, to calculate a comprehensive score for each project. This helps in evaluating and comparing projects based on their financial merits.
context_summary: - Weighted Score assigns weights to financial considerations.
- It evaluates projects based on NPV, ROI, and payback period.

nodes.name: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
nodes.excerpt: The Work Breakdown Structure is a deliverable-oriented grouping of project work defining the total scope.
nodes.notes:
The Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented grouping of the work involved in a project that defines the total scope of the project. It breaks down all work into discrete tasks and is presented in graphical or tabular form. A good WBS is mutually exclusive and completely exhaustive.

The WBS 100% Rule states that once all work for the work packages is completed, the project should be done. Work packages are deliverables, and interim deliverables are needed to create the final product but are discarded after project completion.
nodes.context_summary:
- A deliverable-oriented grouping of project work.
- Defines the total scope of the project.
- Breaks down work into discrete tasks.
- Presented in graphical or tabular form.
- Follows the 100% Rule for project completion.
